lead: A hollow metal pipe a few centimetres across carries microwave power with very little loss. It cannot carry a plain wave like a coaxial cable: the field must fit the metal walls, so only certain patterns — modes — survive, and each mode has a cutoff frequency below which it dies away. The pipe dimensions and two integers called mode indices set that cutoff, the guide wavelength and the wave velocities. Waveguides feed horn antennas and form the bench hardware of every microwave laboratory.
prereq: You need: the propagation constant, phase velocity and wavelength of 1.1, plus basic electromagnetics (Maxwell's equations and the boundary condition on a conductor).

sections.h3: Why a hollow pipe has modes

blocks.text: In free space a wave can travel in any direction with any wavelength. Inside a hollow metal guide it cannot: the tangential electric field must vanish on a perfect conductor, so the field across the guide is pinned at both walls and settles into a standing-wave pattern, like a rope fixed at both ends.

Only patterns that fit exactly survive. Two integers label each one: m counts half-cycles of field variation along the broad wall a (metres), n along the narrow wall b (metres). That gives two families:

items: TE modes (transverse electric): Ez = 0, Hz ≠ 0 — no electric field along the guide axis.
TM modes (transverse magnetic): Hz = 0, Ez ≠ 0 — no magnetic field along the axis.
TEM is impossible: it needs two separate conductors, as in a coaxial cable, not one hollow pipe.

blocks.text: Every mode has a cutoff frequency fc. Below fc the wave does not travel: the fields decay exponentially along the guide and the mode is evanescent. At fc the wave just grazes across the guide. Above fc it propagates. A waveguide is a high-pass device: it passes every frequency above the cutoff of the mode being used and rejects everything below.

Field plots show field lines in cross-section. For TE10 the electric field runs across the narrow wall, is strongest at the centre of the broad wall and zero at its edges. Wall current density is J_s = n̂ × H, so current lines cross the field lines at right angles: in TE10 the current runs from the centre of one broad wall to its edge, across the side wall, and back along the other broad wall. A longitudinal seam along the centre of the broad wall cuts no current; seams and flanges that do interrupt current must be electrically tight.

blocks.text: Two velocities describe the wave. Phase velocity vp is the speed of a point of constant phase; group velocity vg is the speed of the energy and of the modulation:

blocks.where: vp, vg in m/s. Near cutoff vp is far above c and vg near zero; far above cutoff both approach c/√εr.
η = 377/√εr Ω is the filling's intrinsic impedance; ηTE is above η, ηTM below.

blocks.text: The lowest cutoff belongs to TE10: fc10 = c/(2a√εr). It is the dominant mode, the one a practical guide carries alone. Next come TE20 at c/(a√εr) and TE01 at c/(2b√εr); choosing b < a/2 pushes TE01 above TE20 and gives a single-mode band from fc10 to 2fc10. TM11 sits higher, at (c/(2√εr))·√(1/a² + 1/b²). Inside that band the guide gives one field pattern, one λg, one wave impedance; above it two or more modes travel at different velocities and the signal smears.
A circular guide of radius a (metres) uses cylindrical field patterns and Bessel functions in place of sines. Its cutoff is set by a Bessel root:

blocks.where: p is the Bessel root for the chosen TEnm or TMnm mode, from the table; a in metres; c = 3×10⁸ m/s.

blocks.text: TE11 is dominant but a poor mode to rely on: two polarisations share its cutoff, and a slight bend or ovality makes the pattern rotate. Circular guide is used where the joint must turn — rotating radar joints, feeds to parabolic dishes (Unit 3, Aperture and horn antennas) — or where one mode's loss is unusually low. The circular TE01 mode has wall loss that falls as frequency rises, so it suits long high-power runs. A round guide is stiff and easy to machine; electrically it needs a mode suppressor or taper to keep the two TE11 polarisations apart. Rectangular guide stays the bench default: clean mode spacing, polarisation fixed by the walls.

figure.caption: Guide wavelength divided by free-space wavelength for TE10, plotted against f/fc. Just above cutoff λg/λ0 is very large and it tends to infinity at fc; the ratio falls steeply as f rises above cutoff and flattens out toward 1 far above cutoff, where the guide behaves almost like free space.

spec.title: TE10 guide wavelength
spec.aria: TE10 guide wavelength falls toward the free-space wavelength as frequency rises above cutoff.

examples.question: An air-filled rectangular waveguide has broad wall a = 2.286 cm and narrow wall b = 1.016 cm. (a) Find the cutoff frequency of TE10, TE20 and TE01. (b) At 10 GHz find the guide wavelength of TE10 and its wave impedance. Take c = 3×10⁸ m/s and η = 377 Ω.
steps: a = 0.02286 m, b = 0.01016 m; air filling, so εr = 1.
Order 6.56 < 13.12 < 14.76 GHz, so the single-mode band is 6.56 to 13.12 GHz.
10 GHz lies in the band, so only TE10 propagates.
examples.answer: fc10 = 6.56 GHz, fc20 = 13.12 GHz, fc01 = 14.76 GHz; at 10 GHz only TE10 propagates, with λg = 3.98 cm and wave impedance 500 Ω.

traps: Using λ0 where λg is needed. Phase shift along a guide is 2π per λg, not per λ0, so a guide section is longer than the free-space path for the same shift.
Saying a mode 'does not exist' below cutoff. It is evanescent: the field decays as e^(−αz) and carries no real power.
Writing a TM mode with m = 0 or n = 0. Ez ∝ sin(mπx/a)·sin(nπy/b) vanishes if either index is zero, so TM11 is the lowest TM mode.
Swapping a and b. The broad wall a sets fc10; using b is wrong by more than a factor of two for standard X-band guide.
Forgetting √εr. A filling of εr = 4 halves fc and shortens λg.

quiz.q: Define TE and TM modes in a waveguide and state which field component is zero in each.
quiz.a: TE (transverse electric): Ez = 0, Hz ≠ 0. TM (transverse magnetic): Hz = 0, Ez ≠ 0. Each mode keeps the fields transverse to the direction of propagation plus one axial component.

quiz.q: Why can a hollow rectangular waveguide not support a TEM mode?
quiz.a: A TEM mode has no axial field components, so its transverse electric field must come from a two-dimensional potential obeying Laplace's equation with the potential constant on the entire conducting boundary. Laplace's equation then forces the potential to be constant everywhere inside, so the field is zero. Physically, TEM needs two separate conductors at different potentials; one hollow pipe is a single conductor.

quiz.q: Explain why λg is always greater than λ0, and what happens as f approaches fc.
quiz.a: λg = λ0/√(1 − (fc/f)²), and the denominator is below 1 for f > fc, so λg > λ0. As f → fc the denominator tends to zero and λg → ∞: the wave grazes across the guide instead of travelling along it, vp → ∞ and vg → 0.

quiz.q: For the guide of the worked example (a = 2.286 cm, b = 1.016 cm, air filled), find the cutoff frequency of the TE11 mode.
A circular air-filled waveguide has radius 1 cm. Find the cutoff frequency of its dominant mode. Take the Bessel root for TE11 as 1.841 and c = 3×10⁸ m/s.
quiz.a: fc = p·c/(2πa) = 1.841 × 3×10⁸/(2π × 0.01) = 8.79×10⁹ Hz = 8.79 GHz. TE11 is dominant because 1.841 is the smallest root.

quiz.q: A guide is used at a frequency just 2% above fc10. Give two practical problems that follow from the formulas for vp, vg and wave impedance.
quiz.a: √(1 − (fc/f)²) = √(1 − 0.961) ≈ 0.196. λg is about 5λ0, so a short mechanical length spans many electrical wavelengths and tolerance errors matter. vp ≈ 5c, so a small frequency shift swings the phase widely and ruins narrowband matching. vg ≈ 0.2c: energy crawls and group delay is large. TE wave impedance ≈ 377/0.196 ≈ 1920 Ω, far from a 50 Ω source, so transition loss is high.

quiz.q: Show that vp·vg = c²/εr for any TE or TM mode, and say what this means physically.
quiz.a: With s = √(1 − (fc/f)²), vp = c/(√εr·s) and vg = (c/√εr)·s. Multiplying cancels s: vp·vg = c²/εr, independent of mode, dimensions and frequency. The wave inside is a pair of plane waves zig-zagging between the walls; the phase outruns the energy along the axis, the energy moves slower, and the product stays at the plane-wave value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Rectangular guide remains the low-loss choice: satellite payloads use dip-brazed aluminium guide, and 77 GHz radar uses narrow guide machined to tight tolerance. Substrate-integrated waveguide (SIW) builds a rectangular guide from two rows of plated vias in a printed board, so the same cutoff and λg formulas carry over to planar circuits. Overmoded corrugated circular guide carries megawatts in tokamak heating, where the low-loss TE01 mode is chosen deliberately.
